name: Mere Exposure Effect
authorsSource: Robert Zajonc (1968), 'Attitudinal Effects of Mere Exposure'
shortSummary: Repeated exposure tends to increase familiarity and liking.
whyItMatters: Supports repeated touchpoints before the ask.
thirtySecondReelScript: Consistent exposure can make a brand feel more known and safer to engage with.

name: Peak-End Rule
authorsSource: Kahneman and colleagues; peak-end rule research
shortSummary: People often remember an experience mostly by its emotional peak and its ending.
whyItMatters: Supports stronger event peaks and stronger closes.
fifteenSecondScript: People remember the peak and the ending.
thirtySecondReelScript: A webinar is not remembered evenly. The intense moment and the ending shape what stays with the prospect.

name: Endowment Effect
authorsSource: Thaler; Kahneman, Knetsch, & Thaler (1990), endowment effect
shortSummary: People often value something more once they feel ownership over it.
thirtySecondReelScript: When the experience feels like mine instead of generic, movement often becomes more likely.

shortSummary: Effort often accelerates as people feel closer to a goal.
whyItMatters: Supports progress-based nurture and event-pass movement.
thirtySecondReelScript: People move faster when they feel closer to completion.

name: Loss Aversion
authorsSource: Kahneman & Tversky (1979), Prospect Theory / loss aversion
shortSummary: People tend to feel losses more strongly than equivalent gains.
whyItMatters: Supports cost-of-delay messaging and missed-opportunity follow-up.
thirtySecondReelScript: Sometimes the strongest frame is not only what they gain, but what they keep losing by waiting or leaking.

name: Implementation Intentions
shortSummary: People follow through more often when they form a clear if-then plan in advance.
whyItMatters: Supports pre-webinar nurture, reminders, anticipation, and mental preparation before the event.
fifteenSecondScript: People act better when the action feels mentally prepared, not vague.
thirtySecondReelScript: A lot of webinar owners lose before the webinar ever starts. Research on implementation intentions shows that when people decide in advance what they'll do and when they'll do it, follow-through improves. That's why nurture before the event matters so much.
clipHook: People don't show up sold. They show up warmed.

authorsSource: Reber, Schwarz, & Winkielman (2004), processing fluency research
shortSummary: Information that is easier to process often feels more believable or trustworthy.
whyItMatters: Supports message matching and synchronized experience design.
thirtySecondReelScript: Clear language and consistent steps reduce friction and make trust easier.

name: Choice Overload
shortSummary: Too many options can reduce action compared with a smaller, clearer set.
whyItMatters: Supports simplified offer design and clearer landing pages.
fifteenSecondScript: More options can mean less action.
thirtySecondReelScript: Clean next steps often outperform cluttered decision trees.

name: Foot-in-the-Door Effect
shortSummary: When people agree to a small request first, they become more likely to agree to a larger request later.
whyItMatters: Supports invitation design, comment-to-DM flow, and micro-commitments before bigger asks.
fifteenSecondScript: A small yes makes a bigger yes easier later.
thirtySecondReelScript: Small commitments make bigger commitments easier. Psychologists call this the foot-in-the-door effect. That's why I don't ask cold people for the biggest commitment first. I ask for the hand raise first.
clipHook: A stranger becomes a buyer one commitment at a time.
